questions.q: Roughly how much age gap separates the four OLTP platforms from the four cloud warehouses covered in this course?
options: Two to three decades — the OLTP platforms trace to the 1980s-90s, the warehouses to the 2010s
They were all built in roughly the same decade
The cloud warehouses are actually older than the OLTP platforms
There is no meaningful age difference between them
questions.explain: SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL date to the 1980s-90s; Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, and Redshift were all built in the 2010s — roughly two to three decades later.

questions.q: Why does being 'designed later' tend to produce more convergence toward the ANSI standard?
options: The SQL:2003 standard and decades of join-syntax consensus were already settled by the time the warehouses were built, so they could simply adopt the winning answer
Later platforms are required by law to follow the ANSI standard exactly
Newer platforms have no choice but to copy whichever platform came immediately before them
Convergence is unrelated to when a platform was designed
questions.explain: By the 2010s, SQL:2003 window functions and ANSI join syntax were already public and battle-tested, so newer platforms didn't have to re-litigate those design decisions.

questions.q: Why does Oracle still support the legacy (+) join operator and the DUAL table today?
options: Backward compatibility — decades of production Oracle code depends on them, so removing them would break existing systems
Because ANSI standard syntax doesn't work on Oracle at all
Because Oracle customers specifically prefer (+) and DUAL over modern syntax
Because Oracle has no alternative syntax available
questions.explain: Both (+) and DUAL are real design decisions made before today's consensus existed; Oracle keeps them working because deleting them would break decades of existing production code.

questions.q: Which platform in this chapter is literally built on a fork of another OLTP-era platform, inheriting its modern syntax wholesale?
options: Redshift, built on an older fork of PostgreSQL
Snowflake, built on a fork of Oracle
BigQuery, built on a fork of MySQL
Databricks SQL, built on a fork of T-SQL
questions.explain: Redshift is PostgreSQL-derived, built on an older Postgres fork, so it inherited PostgreSQL's already-modern, standards-aligned syntax rather than evolving its own from scratch.

questions.q: What is the core pattern this lesson identifies as the reason warehouse dialects converge more than OLTP dialects do?
options: Warehouses were designed after the standard existed and have little legacy installed base to protect, while OLTP platforms predate the standard and must preserve old quirks for backward compatibility
Warehouse dialects are simpler and have fewer features overall
OLTP platforms were designed by committee while warehouses were designed by a single vendor
There is no real pattern — the convergence is coincidental
questions.explain: The lesson's core claim: OLTP platforms carry pre-standard design decisions locked in by backward compatibility, while cloud warehouses, built later with the standard already settled, converge toward it and each other instead.
